en: The Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of the Retribution for Violating the Precepts, spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time...

Then, at the time of the afternoon, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana arose from his meditative concentration and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have a doubt and now wish to inquire about it.
I only pray that you will grant me your permission.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"I shall listen to your question;
I will explain it for you.
Maudgalyāyana then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī lacks a sense of shame and dread of blame, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and violates the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma), as well as the prādeśanika, pāyattika, sthūlātyaya, saṃghāvaśeṣa, and pārājika offenses—how many unwholesome transgressions do they incur?”
“I only wish that you would explain this.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively.”
I shall explain this for you.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī is without shame or remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and violates the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharmas),
they will fall into hell for a duration equal to five hundred years of the Four Heavenly Kings’ lifespan, which, by human calculation, is nine hundred thousand years.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"One who is shameless and lacks remorse, who treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and arrogance, commits a *pātideśanīya* offense.
As for the lifespan of one thousand years among the Trāyastriṃśa devas, when one falls into hell, it corresponds to three hundred and sixty million years by human reckoning."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"To be without shame or remorse, to treat the Buddha’s words with contempt, and to commit an offense—this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
As for the lifespan in the Yāma Heaven, which is two thousand years, one who falls into hell will remain there for twenty-four billion human years."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Being shameless and lacking remorse, and thus treating the Buddha’s words with contempt, one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
A lifespan of four thousand years in the Tuṣita Heaven corresponds to fifty billion and sixty thousand years by human reckoning when one falls into hell."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "To be without shame or remorse,
to treat the Buddha’s words with contempt, and to commit an offense against the Saṃghāvaśeṣa— such as this,
one will fall into hell for the lifespan of eight thousand years of the Nirmāṇarati devas, which, by human reckoning, is two hundred thirty billion and forty thousand years."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"One who is shameless and lacks remorse, who treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and arrogance, commits a pārājika offense.

Such a person will fall into hell for a lifespan of sixteen thousand years as measured by the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; in human reckoning, this is nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand years."
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Maudgalyāyana spoke these verses:
"Because of the causes and conditions of contempt, One falls into the evil realms at the end of life."
Those who cultivate goodness through causes and conditions will, upon death, be born in the heavens.
By virtue of this cultivation of meritorious deeds, they leave evil behind and attain liberation;
yet those who do not correctly contemplate causes and conditions fall into the evil realms when the body perishes.
The bhikṣu who is heedful finds joy; the negligent have much sorrow and reproach.
A dispute that begins small leads to great ruin; by accumulating evil, one enters the blazing fire.
Upholding the precepts brings the merit of joy; breaking the precepts brings a heart of fear.
Having forever severed the outflows of the three realms, one then attains nirvāṇa.
The virtue of precepts is worthy of reliance; the retribution of merit constantly follows oneself.
Seeing the Dharma, one becomes a leader among men; the multitude stays far from the three evil paths.
Vigilance in the precepts removes fear; such merit and virtue are honored throughout the three realms.
Ghosts, dragons, snakes, and venomous creatures do not harm one who upholds the precepts.
Even the divine seers and those with the five supernatural powers, who have created various worldly incantations and arts, [cannot prevail].
For the sake of those possessing shame and remorse, To sever all lack of shame and remorse,
The Tathāgata has established the prohibitive precepts, Reciting them every half-month;
Having explained the benefits of the precepts, I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas.
The Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of the Retribution for Violating the Precepts Spoken by the Buddha.
